issues.legal_issue: A civil suit is barred when its substance and likely effect would indirectly set aside or modify a proceeding or order under the tax statute.
material_facts: Assets including the disputed gold ornaments were seized and retained following a search and an order made in tax proceedings.
The plaintiff claimed a share in the ornaments and sought partition of them, although the other family members did not dispute her claim.
A decree in the suit would remove the ornaments from the tax retention process and affect their availability for application toward tax liabilities.
The plaintiff had not used the statutory procedure for objecting to the retention order.
issues.conclusion: The partition suit was barred because a decree in it would have the effect of modifying the tax proceedings and order; the lower courts’ decisions were set aside and the suit was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 293 of the Income Tax Act, 1961, expressly bars a civil suit whose effect is to set aside or modify a proceeding taken or order made under the Act; its expanded wording is not confined to directly challenging an order. The substance and ultimate effect of the suit, rather than its form or the relief as framed, govern. Under Section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure, civil jurisdiction is excluded where the statute expressly bars it. The Court applied the principles in Dulhabhai v. State of Madhya Pradesh, particularly the principle concerning an express bar, and relied on Raleigh Investment Co. Ltd. v. Governor-General in Council, Kamala Mills Ltd. v. State of Bombay, and Rangammal v. Union of India for examining the substance and effect of a suit.

predicates.civil_suit: A claimant brought a civil suit concerning property that had been seized and retained in tax proceedings.
predicates.decree_would_remove_seized_assets_from_t: The decree sought would remove the seized property from the tax process or otherwise affect the operation of the tax proceeding or order.
predicates.civil_suit_is_barred: The civil suit cannot be maintained.

issues.definition: When a civil suit seeks a decree that would remove seized assets from tax proceedings, the suit is barred.

issues.legal_issue: A third party claiming an interest in seized assets may object to the order retaining them under the statutory objection procedure.
material_facts: The tax authority seized and retained the ornaments after finding them in the possession or control of a taxpayer.
The plaintiff claimed that the ornaments belonged to her mother and that she was entitled to a share in them.
The plaintiff knew of the tax proceedings, sought return of the ornaments from the tax authority, and did not apply to the designated tax authority to object to the retention order.
The tax officer was not satisfied that the ornaments were held for another person.
issues.conclusion: The statutory objection procedure was available to a third party, because the provision applies to “any person”; the plaintiff could have used it. The tax officer was not required to proceed against her as another person under the separate provision for that purpose when not satisfied that the assets were held on another person’s behalf.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 132(7) and 132(11) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, govern, respectively, action where the tax officer is satisfied that seized assets are held for another person and objections to an order made concerning seized assets. The words “any person” in Section 132(11) include a third party who objects to the retention order and seeks appropriate relief.

predicates.third_party_claims_an_interest_in_seized: A person other than the person subjected to the search claims an interest in property seized during the search.
predicates.retention_order_made: The tax authority made an order retaining the seized property.
predicates.third_party_may_object_to_retention_orde: The third party may seek relief by objecting to the retention order through the statutory objection procedure.

issues.definition: A third party claiming an interest in seized property may object to its retention when an order retaining it has been made.
